abstract: Presents SafeAgent, a runtime security architecture that treats agent safety as a stateful decision problem over evolving interaction trajectories rather than single-turn input-output filtering. It separates execution governance from semantic risk reasoning via two coordinated components: a Runtime Controller that mediates actions around the agent loop (governed tool access, context override, replanning, rollback, safe-mode termination, tool-argument rewriting, human-in-the-loop) and a context-aware decision Core formalized as a context-aware Advanced Machine Intelligence (AMI) system with operators for risk encoding, utility-cost evaluation, consequence (world-model) modeling, policy arbitration, and state synchronization. Evaluated on Agent Security Bench (ASB) and InjecAgent against direct/indirect prompt injection and memory poisoning; reduces ASB attack success rates (IPI ASR 0.2936, MP ASR 0.1858) and drives InjecAgent data-stealing S1/S2 to 0.0000.

title: PARSE: Provenance-Aware Retrieval Sanitization for Professional Domain LLM Agents
abstract: Demonstrates that prompt-injection defenses evaluated on synthetic benchmarks do not generalize to real enterprise documents, using a real-document benchmark of 122 tasks across five professional domains (financial, legal, medical, scientific, DevOps) built from actual SEC filings, Federal Register rules, PubMed abstracts, arXiv papers, and GitHub postmortems with domain-camouflaged injection payloads. Paraphrasing, the strongest synthetic-benchmark defense, shows no statistically significant attack-success reduction on real documents (p=0.500) while degrading utility 91.8%->82.8%. Introduces PARSE, a six-component inference-time, training-free, provenance-aware fact-preserving sanitization pipeline (domain classifier, directiveness gate, combined tagger-extractor, structure-aware paraphraser, consistency checker, output builder) that achieves 15.6% ASR (38% reduction vs 25.4% baseline, p=0.014) at 86.9% utility -- the only condition both statistically significant and near-baseline utility.

title: Defense Effectiveness Across Architectural Layers: A Mechanistic Evaluation of Persistent Memory Attacks on Stateful LLM Agents
abstract: First systematic evaluation of defense effectiveness against persistent (delayed-trigger) memory attacks on stateful LLM agents. Evaluates six defenses across four architectural layers (input, retrieval, instruction, tool) against delayed-trigger attacks on nine open-source models (5,040 runs, N=40/condition, 108 pre-specified comparisons, BCa bootstrap CIs, Holm-Bonferroni). Four defenses (input-level Minimizer/Sanitizer, retrieval-level RAG Sanitizer/RAG LLM Judge) fail at 88-89% ASR, statistically indistinguishable from the 88.6% undefended baseline; Prompt Hardening partially fails (77.8%). Only tool-gating at the memory layer (Memory Sandbox, removing recall capability) reduces ASR to 0% for eight of nine models at zero utility cost. The exception inverts: qwq:32b achieves 0% ASR under no-defense via execution refusal but 100% ASR under Memory Sandbox because removing recall forces it onto the fresh-RAG pathway. Frontier screening: Claude Sonnet 4.6 resists injection entirely (0%), Claude Haiku 4.5 detects and stores a security alert instead of the payload (0% attack).

title: SafeClawBench: Separating Semantic, Audit-Evidence, and Sandbox Harm in Tool-Using LLM Agents
org: Peking University; Beijing Jiaotong University; SUIBE; Huawei; Tsinghua University
abstract: Tool-using LLM agents introduce security failures beyond unsafe text: disclosing protected objects, persistent memory writes, harmful tool/state effects. Existing evals collapse staged attacks into a single attack success rate. SafeClawBench is a staged benchmark with 600 controlled adversarial tasks across six attack families (direct/indirect prompt injection, tool-return injection, memory poisoning, memory extraction, ambiguity-driven unsafe inference). It reports three separate endpoints: semantic attack acceptance, audit-visible harm evidence, and sandbox-observed tool/state harm. Five agent endpoints under four prompt policies; semantic failure rates 9.0%-44.2%; in a 12,000-row matched analysis 291 of 347 observed sandbox harms occur in rows passing the semantic check.

title: SkillVetBench: LLM-as-Judge for Multi-Dimensional Security Risk Evaluation in Open-Source LLM Agent Skills
org: SUPREME Lab, University of Texas at El Paso
abstract: Open-source LLM agent ecosystems grow rapidly but community-contributed skills (modular tool definitions) remain unvetted. Existing scanners operate at the code layer and are blind to instruction-layer and multi-agent risk. SkillVetBench is a public Hugging Face leaderboard using an LLM-as-Judge to vet agent skills. Introduces SARS (Skill Agentic Risk Score), a five-dimensional agentic-risk metric; integrates full CVSS v4.0 vector decomposition and a ClawHub dual-view that places the LLM-generated review beside the official marketplace verdict. LLM-as-Judge achieves zero false negatives across 78 confirmed-malicious skills and zero false positives across 22 benign controls; best static baseline (SkillSieve) misses 15%; for Prompt Injection and Memory Poisoning conventional tools miss 89-100% of threats (CodeBERT detects none of nine memory-poisoning skills). Detection rate varies 35-95% across four LLM evaluators, motivating ensemble scoring.

title: Beyond Pass/Fail: Using Process Mining to Understand How LLMs Resist (and Fail) Red Team Attacks
abstract: Standard AI red teaming reduces adversarial campaigns to a single binary outcome (attack success rate, ASR), ignoring the sequential structure of how models resist or yield. The paper applies process mining to red teaming traces. A controlled experiment pits 60 HarmBench prompts against GPT-OSS 120B and Llama 3.3 70B using 10 prompt mutation strategies over up to 110 attempts per prompt. From 8,575 scored events it extracts Directly-Follows Graphs (DFGs) and state transition matrices revealing structurally distinct defense profiles invisible to ASR: GPT-OSS exhibits a near-absorbing refusal state ('absorbing wall'), while Llama presents multiple porous escape routes ('porous gate'). Mutator effectiveness is asymmetric across models; time-to-jailbreak distributions differ by an order of magnitude.

title: Analyzing the Narration Gap in LLM-Solver Loops
org: Centrum Wiskunde & Informatica, Amsterdam; Eindhoven University of Technology
abstract: Formal tools (SAT/SMT solvers) are increasingly embedded in LLM reasoning pipelines for safety/security-critical questions formulated in logic. A solver produces a sound, independently verifiable answer, but the soundness guarantee can be lost in the solver-model interaction. The hybrid pipeline has three components: formalizing the question, deciding it, and narrating the result. Prior work studied formalization and decision but not narration — the step turning a formal tool's output into the user answer. The paper models the LLM-solver loop as a verified decision procedure, evaluates five open-source models under prompt injection, and finds certificate gating makes the solver verdict sound while an adversary can INVERT a verified conclusion across phrasings and channels. Hardened prompts reduce injection but cannot eliminate it and still suffer under adaptive attack.

title: SafeSpec: Fast and Safe LLM via Dynamic Reflective Sampling
org: Zhejiang University; Harbin Institute of Technology, Shenzhen; Huawei
abstract: Speculative inference accelerates LLM decoding but provides no inherent safety guarantees; existing safety defenses are largely incompatible with speculative inference. SafeSpec is a safety-aware speculative inference framework that integrates risk estimation directly into the verification process. It attaches a lightweight latent safety head to the target model to jointly evaluate semantic validity and safety in a single forward pass. When unsafe generations are detected, SafeSpec applies rollback and safety-guided reflective multi-sampling to recover safe continuations rather than terminating. Models jailbreak attacks as distributional shifts over generative trajectories. On Qwen3-32B, SafeSpec reduces attack success rates by 15% while preserving a 2.06x inference speedup. Published ICML 2026.

title: GuardNet: Ensemble Strategies of Shallow Neural Networks for Robust Prompt Injection and Jailbreak Detection
org: Quickium Technology Ltd.; Federal University of Sao Carlos (UFSCar); IFSP Piracicaba
abstract: LLMs remain vulnerable to Prompt Injection (PI) and Jailbreak (JB) attacks, and benchmark evaluations may be affected by contamination and partial information leakage. GuardNet is a guardrail system based on an ensemble of shallow neural networks (BiLSTMs) with ~47 million parameters. The work investigates the hypothesis that robustness in adversarial scenarios depends more on the diversity of example coverage and threshold calibration than on model scale. GuardNet achieves competitive performance vs lightweight detectors at low latency (~50ms CPU), though larger LLMs (Mistral-7B, Llama-3.1-8B) achieve superior F1/AUROC on the blind JBB-Behaviors benchmark. GuardNet achieves AUROC 0.747 on the blind dataset (n=200) and F1 0.92 on a proprietary benchmark (n=50).

title: Online Shift Detection and Conformal Adaptation for Deployed Safety Classifiers
abstract: An online monitoring system for distributional shift in deployed LLM safety classifiers using calibrated sequential KS test statistics, with a conformal abstention layer to recover decision thresholds. Pre-registered 4-classifier x 5-shift x 20-seed x 2-window factorial (800 cells) achieves 86.6% valid detection (95% CI [84.1,88.8]), mean latency 39.5 steps at window 100, FAR 2-10%. Validated on synthetic onset, real temporal jailbreaks, and a GCG adversarial demonstration showing successful attacks produce insufficient distributional signal for detection in the target classifier. Weighted conformal recovers up to 39pp coverage for DeBERTa but density-ratio estimation collapses (ESS~300) for other classifiers due to high-dimensional perfect separability; PCA to 32 dims breaks the collapse.

title: MEMBRANE: A Self-Evolving Contrastive Safety Memory for LLM Agent Defense
org: KAIST AI; KakaoBank Financial Tech Lab
abstract: MEMBRANE is a self-evolving external guardrail built on Contrastive Safety Memory (CSM): each cell pairs the conditions for blocking a harmful query with those for permitting a superficially similar benign request, indexed by underlying attack strategy so one cell generalizes across topical variants of the same mechanism. Without retraining, MEMBRANE evolves CSM via experience-driven create/update/delete. Across model-level safety on HarmBench and agent-level safety on AgentHarm, it achieves the highest F1 on all six jailbreak attacks, keeps benign refusal on AgentHarm at 7-14% (vs 28-85% for prior guards), retains 87-88% F1 under cross-attack transfer, and remains stable under 20% memory poisoning (ASR drift below 1 point). Motivates with AISI 2026 evaluations reporting Claude Mythos Preview and GPT-5.5 autonomously executing 32-step cyberattacks in controlled settings.

title: Can Data Work be Reparative?
abstract: An ethnographic study (April-December 2024, 12 interviews + 8 months immersion) of Tattle Civic Tech, an India-based civic-tech initiative building online-safety datasets collaboratively from a feminist perspective with those most impacted by online harms (oGBV, hate, sexual violence). Examines two dataset projects -- a gendered-slur lexicon in four Indian languages (650+ entries Hindi/Tamil/Malayalam/Indian English) and a Hindi LLM safety benchmark (2000 prompts, hate + sex-related crimes) contributed as a pilot to MLCommons' AILuminate v1.0 AI Safety benchmark. Through an STS lens of reparative justice, argues the work of repairing data work lies in resetting the relations of accountability in AI, and surfaces tensions in just reward, recognition, and collective dataset governance. To FAccT 2026.

title: The Almost Intelligent Revolution: Options for Scaling Up Deliberation and Empowering People with AI
abstract: A book chapter (Handbook of Democracy in the Era of Artificial Intelligence, 2026) exploring how LLMs can scale up and democratise deliberation while introducing biases, sycophancy, and hallucinations that distort it. Drawing on Systemic-Functional Linguistics, examines how variation across language users and language use shapes participation in AI-supported deliberation. Reviews deliberation studies (Habermas Machine on 5,734 UK residents; Jungherr-Rauchfleisch AI-penalty study on 1,850 German participants; iDem text-simplification project where 92-96% of EU Parliament/UN sentences required simplification) and assesses potential to scaffold argument and reduce exclusionary linguistic norms, while cautioning against overclaiming (unrealistic expectations) and underclaiming (missed opportunities).

title: KVEraser: Learning to Steer KV Cache for Efficient Localized Context Erasing
abstract: KVEraser is a learned KV-cache editing method for efficient localized post-hoc context erasing. A local edit to a processed context has a global consequence: once a span is processed its influence propagates into cached states of all subsequent tokens, so exact erasing must recompute all tokens after the deleted span. KVEraser replaces only the KV states of the erased interval with learned steering states while reusing the remaining cache, via a two-stage pipeline (generic span-neighbor pre-training + task-specific fine-tuning). Motivated by long-context LLM applications where stale retrieved facts, incorrect tool observations, retracted user preferences, or harmful prompt injections in imported skill files are identified only after prefill. Nearly matches full recomputation across 1K-32K contexts while latency increases only 24% vs 17.6x for full recompute; generalizes to unseen long-document QA with harmful factual distractors at 3-4x speedup over recomputation.

title: DoubtProbe: Black-Box Jailbreak Defense via Structural Verification and Semantic Auditing
org: East China Normal University; HKUST(GZ); Institute of Information Engineering, CAS
abstract: DoubtProbe is a dual-branch inference-time black-box jailbreak defense combining structural verification (extract a structured representation S from request Q, reconstruct Q-hat from S only, and detect information-preservation failures via a Comparator) with semantic auditing (direct unsafe-intent verdict on Q). The key observation is that many black-box jailbreaks do not remove the harmful goal but reorganize the information needed to express it, evading safety alignment while remaining recoverable. Formulated as consistency checking under controlled transformation. On Qwen2.5-72B it reduces JBB artifact ASR from 0.293 to 0.100 and CodeAttack ASR from 0.152 to 0.001, with benign macro FPR 0.019; pattern stable on Llama-3.1-70B.

title: Defending Jailbreak Attacks on Large Language Models via Manifold Trajectory Kinetics
org: Huazhong University of Science and Technology; Changsha University of Science and Technology; Xiangtan University; City University of Macau; Griffith University
abstract: Prior jailbreak detectors assume benign and jailbreak prompts are linearly separable in a fixed metric space (raw inputs, gradients, or hidden features). This breaks under (i) pseudo-malicious prompts (PMPs) — benign-by-intent prompts containing safety-related keywords — and (ii) detector-aware adaptive attacks. MTK (Manifold Trajectory Kinetics) treats an LLM as a kinetic system and tracks how a prompt's neighborhood (benign-neighbor rank) structure evolves across layers; jailbreak prompts exhibit a 'bumping' trajectory near malicious seeds that later shifts toward benign neighborhoods to evade refusal. MTK reaches jailbreak TPR 95% at FPR 5% on benign and 2% FPR on PMPs; under adaptive attacks TPR 85% (eASR<=0.2). Mean AUROC 0.940 across 10 attacks x 4 LLMs; extends to VLMs.

title: Defending against Adaptive Prompt Injection Attacks via Reasoning-enabled Task Alignment
org: University of Waterloo; Zhejiang University; KTH Royal Institute of Technology
abstract: Indirect prompt injection (PI) hijacks LLM agents by embedding malicious instructions in third-party data retrieved during tool execution. Existing defenses report near-zero ASR on static benchmarks but collapse under adaptive attacks (per-defense highest ASR rises 15.8 percentage points static->adaptive). Two failure modes: (1) observation-level defenses recognize specific injection patterns instead of checking whether each embedded instruction is relevant to the user task (evadable by reformulation: Contextual Hijacking, Lexical Camouflage, Canary-Blind Entanglement, Phantom Continuation); (2) adversarial training mode-collapses onto a few templates lacking strategy coverage. RETA grounds defense in user-task alignment via chain-of-thought reasoning at each tool-output step, trained with diversity-rewarded adversarial RL. Keeps per-task adaptive ASR <10%, average adaptive ASR 2.92%/3.75% on Qwen3-4B/Llama-3.1-8B while preserving UA/BU.

title: CodeSentinel: A Three-Layer Defense Against Indirect Prompt Injection in Code Contexts
org: National Yang Ming Chiao Tung University; Hon Hai Research Institute
abstract: Code LLMs retrieve external code context from repositories, documentation, issue threads, and coding-agent environments, creating an indirect-prompt-injection surface where attackers hide instructions in comments, strings, identifiers, or decoy code. CodeSentinel is a three-layer inference-time sanitizer using Tree-sitter to extract high-risk model-facing CST nodes, then combines syntax-guided pre-filtering, CST-guided Dynamic Min-K% scoring, and node perturbation analysis to detect adversarial and natural-looking semantic triggers. Detected nodes are removed/neutralized before reaching the downstream Code LLM. Across six recent attack families CodeSentinel achieves 0.80 average node-level F1 (AUROC 0.82), outperforming CodeGarrison (0.70), DePA (0.51), KillBadCode (0.30); reduces sample-level ASR on open/commercial victims (e.g. Claude-3.5-Haiku 27.11%->7.72%).

title: ShieldNet: Network-Level Guardrails against Emerging Supply-Chain Injections in Agentic Systems
org: UIUC; University of Chicago; University of Georgia; United States Military Academy; eBay; Johns Hopkins University; UCSB; Virtue AI
abstract: As agents increasingly rely on third-party tools and MCP servers, a new class of supply-chain threats emerges where malicious behaviors are embedded in seemingly benign tools, preserving benign interfaces and I/O while hiding harmful logic at runtime, leading to sensitive data leakage or unauthorized actions. Existing MCP scanners and semantic guardrails perform poorly due to stealthiness. SC-Inject-Bench: large-scale supply-chain benchmark with 10,000+ malicious MCP tools in a taxonomy of 25+ attack types derived from MITRE ATT&CK (109 servers, 984 tools, 30 techniques, 19,961 validated executions). ShieldNet is a network-level guardrail integrating a MITM proxy + event extractor to identify critical network behaviors, then a lightweight post-trained guardrail model (Qwen3-0.6B) for detection. Achieves up to 0.995 F-1 with 0.8% false positives, low runtime overhead.

title: Prompt Injection Attack to Tool Selection in LLM Agents
org: Huazhong University of Science and Technology; Duke University; Lehigh University
abstract: Introduces ToolHijacker, the first prompt injection attack targeting tool selection (retrieval+selection) in LLM agents under a no-box scenario. ToolHijacker injects a single malicious tool document into the tool library to compel the agent to consistently choose the attacker's tool for a target task. Crafting the malicious document is formulated as a two-phase optimization (retrieval objective R + selection objective S) solved by gradient-free and gradient-based methods. Evaluated on MetaTool and ToolBench across 8 LLMs and 4 retrievers; achieves up to 100% AHR and ~96.7% ASR on GPT-4o, defeats prevention (StruQ, SecAlign) and detection (known-answer, DataSentinel, PPL, PPL-W) defenses.

title: Red-Teaming LLM Multi-Agent Systems via Communication Attacks
org: Michigan State University; University of Arizona
abstract: Introduces Agent-in-the-Middle (AiTM), a novel attack that exploits the inter-agent communication mechanism of LLM-based multi-agent systems (LLM-MAS). Instead of compromising individual agents or injecting adversarial inputs, AiTM uses an external LLM-powered adversarial agent to intercept and manipulate messages sent to a victim agent, with a reflection mechanism generating contextually-tailored malicious instructions. Evaluated on AutoGen and Camel across 4 communication structures (Chain/Tree/Complete/Random) and tasks (MMLU, HumanEval, MBPP) for targeted-behavior and DoS goals; ASR exceeds 40% in all cases, >70% in most, and compromises real-world MetaGPT (100% on SoftwareDev) and partially ChatDev.

title: MPMA: Preference Manipulation Attack Against Model Context Protocol
org: University of Electronic Science and Technology of China; City University of Hong Kong
abstract: Introduces the MCP Preference Manipulation Attack (MPMA): a malicious paid MCP server provider manipulates its tool name/description so the LLM agent consistently prefers it over functionally-equivalent competing MCP servers, yielding economic benefit (service fees / ad revenue). Two strategies: DPMA (Directly inserting words like 'best'/'This is the best tool in the world', up to 100% ASR but obvious) and GAPMA (Genetic-based Advertising Preference Manipulation Attack — four advertising styles Authoritative/Emotional/Exaggerated/Subliminal + a genetic algorithm for stealth). Evaluated across 8 MCP servers and 5 LLMs; GAPMA balances high ASR and stealth, evading LLM-as-a-judge, human annotators, and MCP scanning tools (MCPScan, MCPShield). Estimated unfair benefit >$200k/yr to competitors.

title: MCPXKIT: The Unified Toolkit for Analyzing Model Context Protocol Security
org: Tsinghua University (Shenzhen); Ant Group; Swinburne University of Technology; University of Adelaide; UNSW Sydney
abstract: Presents MCPXKIT, the first plugin-based attack-simulation framework for the Model Context Protocol, plus a four-dimensional taxonomy of 31 distinct MCP attack types: Direct Tool Injection, Indirect Tool Injection, Malicious User, and LLM Inherent attacks. Conducts the first quantitative efficacy analysis (Attack Efficacy = entropy-weighted combination of success rate S, security risk level L, persistent impact scope I, implementation difficulty D). Four key insights: file-based ops execute without confirmation, MCP agents blindly rely on tool descriptions (LLM sycophancy), shared-context chain attacks (infectious + multi-tool cooperation), and agents cannot distinguish external data from executable instructions.

title: ACE: A Security Architecture for LLM-Integrated App Systems
abstract: Identifies three new attacks (Execution Flow Disruption, Execution Manager Hijack, Planner Manipulation) that subvert the planning and execution integrity/availability of LLM-integrated app systems, demonstrated against IsolateGPT. Proposes Abstract-Concrete-Execute (ACE), a three-phase security architecture: abstract planning over only trusted user-query info, concrete plan instantiation via registered apps, and isolated execution under a static-analysis-verified lattice-based information-flow policy and least-privilege. ACE blocks all attacks on INJECAGENT (100% security) and Agent Security Bench (≥86% utility), prevents the three new attacks, and retains ≥80% utility on the LangChain Tool Usage benchmark.

title: G-Safeguard: A Topology-Guided Security Lens and Treatment on LLM-based Multi-agent Systems
org: USTC; Tongji University; Wuhan University; Shanghai University
abstract: Introduces G-Safeguard, a topology-guided security lens and treatment for LLM-based multi-agent systems. It constructs a multi-agent utterance graph capturing inter-agent communication and topology, formulates attack detection as a GNN node-classification (anomaly) problem to pinpoint high-risk/compromised agents, and performs topological intervention (edge pruning) to remediate by blocking malicious-information propagation. Across LLM backbones, MAS frameworks (incl. Camel), and topologies (chain/tree/star/random), G-Safeguard recovers >40% of performance under prompt injection, reduces ASR by 21.38%/22.01% (prompt injection on CSQA/MMLU), 12.67% (tool attack), 16.27% (memory poison), and transfers to large-scale MAS (up to 80 agents) without retraining (39.23% recovery at 65 agents).

title: DataSentinel: A Game-Theoretic Detection of Prompt Injection Attacks
venue: IEEE Symposium on Security and Privacy (S&P) 2025
abstract: DataSentinel fine-tunes a detection LLM via a minimax (game-theoretic) formulation to detect inputs contaminated with injected prompts that are strategically adapted to evade detection. The inner-max optimizes adaptive attacks; the outer-min fine-tunes the detection LLM. Evaluated on 7 tasks, 9 injected datasets, 6 LLMs, 9 existing + 3 adaptive prompt injection attacks; achieves FPR/FNR close to 0 and at most 0.07, outperforming 6 baselines.

title: MELON: Provable Defense Against Indirect Prompt Injection Attacks in AI Agents
abstract: MELON (Masked re-Execution and tooL comparisON) is a training-free indirect-prompt-injection (IPI) defense for LLM agents. It re-executes the agent's trajectory with a masked, task-neutral user prompt and detects an attack when tool calls in the original run match those of the masked run (indicating the action depends on injected content, not the user task). Three designs (custom masking function, tool-call cache, tool-call comparison) reduce FPs/FNs. On AgentDojo across GPT-4o, o3-mini, Llama-3.3-70B, MELON and MELON-Aug outperform 5 SOTA defenses; MELON-Aug reaches 0.32% ASR with 68.72% utility on GPT-4o.

title: IPIGuard: A Novel Tool Dependency Graph-Based Defense Against Indirect Prompt Injection in LLM Agents
venue: Conference on Empirical Methods in Natural Language Processing (EMNLP) 2025
abstract: IPIGuard is an execution-centric IPI defense that models an LLM agent's task execution as traversal over a planned Tool Dependency Graph (TDG). By decoupling action planning from interaction with external data and restricting tool invocations to a pre-approved plan, it prevents injected-instruction-triggered tool calls at the source. Argument Estimation and Node Expansion handle dynamic planning; Fake Tool Invocation handles user/injected task overlap. On AgentDojo across six LLMs and four IPI attacks, IPIGuard achieves the lowest average ASR (<1%) with strong utility.

title: SAGA: A Security Architecture for Governing AI Agentic Systems
venue: Network and Distributed System Security Symposium (NDSS) 2026
abstract: SAGA is a Security Architecture for Governing Agentic systems giving users oversight over their LLM agents' lifecycle. Users register agents with a central Provider holding contact info and user-defined Access Contact Policies; a cryptographic mechanism derives Access Control Tokens (encrypted under a Diffie-Hellman-derived shared key, scoped by expiry and request quota) for fine-grained control over inter-agent communication. Formally verified with ProVerif (Dolev-Yao). Integrates with Google A2A and Model Context Protocol. Evaluated on calendar/email/writing agentic tasks across on-device and cloud LLMs with <0.6% overhead on fast tasks; scales to ~300M agents.

title: MTSA: Multi-turn Safety Alignment for LLMs through Multi-round Red-teaming
org: Harbin Institute of Technology Shenzhen / NTU Singapore / Zhejiang University
venue: Annual Meeting of the Association for Computational Linguistics (ACL) 2025
abstract: MTSA is a two-stage framework securing LLMs against multi-round jailbreaks. Stage 1 (thought-guided attack learning) builds a Think-before-attack dataset and fine-tunes a red-team model. Stage 2 (adversarial iterative optimization) co-evolves the red-team and target models, with a multi-turn RL algorithm based on future rewards for robust safety alignment. The red-team model reaches SOTA attack success while the target model significantly improves multi-turn and single-turn safety without losing generality or over-refusing.

title: Representation Bending for Large Language Model Safety
org: Seoul National University / Yonsei University / AIM Intelligence / University of Michigan / Stanford / Amazon AWS
venue: Annual Meeting of the Association for Computational Linguistics (ACL) 2025
abstract: REPBEND is a fine-tuning approach that disrupts the representations underlying harmful behaviors in LLMs by bending the safe and unsafe representation spaces apart. Extending activation steering into a LoRA fine-tuning loss (retain + forget + cosine + KL terms), REPBEND achieves up to 95% reduction in attack success rates across diverse black-box and white-box jailbreak benchmarks, outperforming Circuit Breaker, RMU, and NPO, with negligible loss of usability/general capability.

title: The Hidden Risks of Large Reasoning Models: A Safety Assessment of R1
org: UC Santa Cruz; UC Berkeley; UC Santa Barbara; Cisco Research
abstract: A comprehensive safety assessment of large reasoning models (LRMs) such as DeepSeek-R1 against established safety benchmarks and adversarial attacks (jailbreak, prompt injection). Four key findings: (1) significant safety gap between open-source reasoning models and o3-mini; (2) stronger reasoning ability increases potential harm of unsafe answers; (3) safety thinking emerges in LRM reasoning but fails against adversarial attacks; (4) the thinking process in R1 poses greater safety concerns than final answers.

title: A Survey on Privacy Risks and Protection in Large Language Models
org: Jimei University; Wenzhou-Kean University; HKUST(GZ); NTU; New York University
venue: Journal of King Saud University - Computer and Information Sciences 2025
abstract: Comprehensive survey of privacy risks in LLMs. Analyzes privacy leakage (sensitive-information leakage, contextual leakage, personal-preferences leakage) and privacy attacks (model-based: backdoor/model-inversion/model-stealing; data-based: data-stealing/training-data-extraction; user-based: membership-inference/attribute-inference). Reviews countermeasures (data cleaning, inference detection, federated learning, differential privacy, cryptography, backdoor removal, confidential computing) and proposes future directions: privacy-preserving model compression, privacy risk assessment, secure knowledge transfer, interdisciplinary governance frameworks.

title: A Survey on Autonomy-Induced Security Risks in Large Model-Based Agents
org: Tsinghua University (Dept. CS&Tech, THBI Lab, Tsinghua-Bosch Joint Center for ML); BNRist Center; RealAI
venue: IEEE Transactions on Pattern Analysis and Machine Intelligence (TPAMI) 2025
abstract: Survey examining structural foundations of large-model agents (memory retention, modular tool use, recursive planning, reflective reasoning) and the qualitatively new security risks autonomy introduces (memory poisoning, tool misuse, reward hacking, emergent misalignment) that extend beyond conventional systems and standalone LLMs. Introduces a five-level autonomy taxonomy, maps risks to a modular agent architecture and across abilities x autonomy levels, formalizes failure modes as Constrained Markov Decision Process (CMDP) constraint violations, reviews a vertically integrated defense stack, and proposes the Reflective Risk-Aware Agent Architecture (R2A2) for intrinsic safety.

title: IS-Bench: Evaluating Interactive Safety of VLM-Driven Embodied Agents in Daily Household Tasks
org: Shanghai Jiao Tong University; Shanghai AI Laboratory; Beihang University; Fudan University
abstract: IS-Bench is the first multi-modal interactive safety benchmark for VLM-driven embodied agents, featuring 161 challenging scenarios with 388 unique safety risks across 10 domestic categories, instantiated in the OmniGibson high-fidelity physics simulator. It introduces process-oriented evaluation that verifies whether risk-mitigation actions are performed in the correct procedural order (before/after risk-prone steps), unlike termination-oriented benchmarks that only check final state. Experiments on 16 VLMs (GPT-4o, Gemini-2.5, Claude-3.7-Sonnet, Qwen2.5-VL, InternVL series, Llama-3.2) show agents lack interactive safety awareness, and safety-aware CoT improves safety but compromises task success.

title: Can We Trust AI Benchmarks? An Interdisciplinary Review of Current Issues in AI Evaluation
abstract: Interdisciplinary meta-review of ~110 studies (Jan 2014-Dec 2024, snowball-sampled, >half from 2023+) on shortcomings of quantitative AI benchmarking. Presents nine interrelated reasons to be cautious with benchmarks: (1) data collection/annotation/documentation problems, (2) weak construct validity & epistemological claims, (3) sociocultural context & gap, (4) narrow diversity & scope, (5) economic/competitive/commercial roots, (6) rigging/gaming/measure-becoming-target, (7) dubious community vetting & path dependencies, (8) rapid development & benchmark saturation, (9) AI complexity & unknown unknowns. Argues AI safety benchmarks must themselves be subjected to the same transparency/fairness/explainability demands as the models they evaluate, especially as the EU AI Act relies on benchmarks for high-risk and GPAI-systemic-risk assessment.

title: Benchmarking LLMs and LLM-based Agents in Practical Vulnerability Detection for Code Repositories
org: National University of Singapore; Institute for Infocomm Research A*STAR; Fudan University; Nanyang Technological University
abstract: Introduces JITVUL, a just-in-time (JIT) vulnerability-detection benchmark linking each function to its vulnerability-introducing and fixing commits, built from 879 CVEs spanning 91 CWEs (1,758 pairwise commits) on top of PrimeVul. Enables pairwise evaluation (vulnerable vs patched-benign versions) and interprocedural context. Evaluates Plain LLM, Dependency-Augmented LLM, and ReAct Agents (with get_callers/get_callees/get_definition tools) across CoT/few-shot prompting and GPT-4o/GPT-4o-mini/Llama-3.1-8B. Finds ReAct Agents leverage thought-action-observation + interprocedural context to better distinguish vulnerable from benign code, but both LLMs and agents show inconsistent analysis (misidentifying vulnerabilities or over-analyzing security guards), indicating significant room for improvement.

title: Foot-In-The-Door: A Multi-turn Jailbreak for LLMs
org: University of Notre Dame; Purdue University; Pennsylvania State University
abstract: FITD is a multi-turn jailbreak leveraging the psychological foot-in-the-door phenomenon: minor initial commitments lower resistance to larger transgressions. The attack progressively escalates malicious intent through intermediate bridge prompts and self-aligns the model's responses to induce toxic outputs. Achieves an average 94% attack success rate across seven widely used models, outperforming SOTA methods. Includes an in-depth analysis of LLM self-corruption.

title: Understanding and Enhancing the Transferability of Jailbreaking Attacks
org: The University of Sydney; Hong Kong Baptist University
abstract: This work analyzes why jailbreaking attacks fail to transfer to proprietary LLMs by examining their impact on the model's intent perception. Adversarial sequences create deceptive high-importance regions that divert the source LLM's focus away from malicious-intent tokens, but fail to mislead target LLMs due to inherent distributional dependency from overfitting source-model parameters. The proposed Perceived-importance Flatten (PiF) method uniformly disperses focus across neutral-intent tokens via synonym token replacement, providing efficient transferable red-teaming evaluation of proprietary LLMs.

title: Adversarial Reasoning at Jailbreaking Time
org: University of Pennsylvania; Robust Intelligence @ Cisco
abstract: Adversarial Reasoning is a gradient-free jailbreaking framework that applies test-time-compute reasoning to exploit a target LLM's loss signal. It formulates jailbreaking as optimizing a reasoning string via three steps — reason (CoT tree), verify (loss-as-process-reward-model score), and search (tree search with backtracking) — realized by Attacker, Feedback, and Refiner LLM modules. Achieves SOTA attack success rates against many aligned and adversarially-trained LLMs, including those that trade inference-time compute for safety, laying the foundation for more robust AI systems.

title: Topic-FlipRAG: Topic-Orientated Adversarial Opinion Manipulation Attacks to Retrieval-Augmented Generation Models
org: Wuhan University; Nanyang Technological University; Worcester Polytechnic Institute
abstract: Topic-FlipRAG is a two-stage adversarial opinion manipulation attack on RAG systems that shifts the stance polarity of model outputs across multiple related topic queries (not single factual queries). Stage 1 (knowledge-guided attack) uses an LLM's internal semantic knowledge to perform stealthy multi-granular edits with polarity control on a target document; Stage 2 uses gradients from an open-source neural ranking model (NRM) to generate an adversarial trigger maximizing retrieval. The poisoned document is injected into the RAG knowledge base. Experiments show significant opinion shifts; existing defenses (perplexity detection, masking, paraphrasing, reranking) are inadequate.

title: LLM-attacker: Enhancing Closed-loop Adversarial Scenario Generation for Autonomous Driving with Large Language Models
org: Tongji University; The Hong Kong Polytechnic University
venue: IEEE Transactions on Intelligent Transportation Systems (TITS) 2025
abstract: LLM-attacker is a closed-loop adversarial scenario generation framework for autonomous driving systems (ADS). Multiple collaborating LLM agents (Initialization, Reflection, Modification) automatically identify optimal adversarial vehicles within complex traffic scenes; their adversarial trajectories are optimized to maximize collision likelihood with the ego vehicle, and scenarios are iteratively refined based on ADS performance for adversarial training. LLM-attacker creates more dangerous scenarios than baseline methods, and ADS trained with it achieves a collision rate half that of training with normal scenarios — supporting safety assurance and policy verification compliant with regulatory standards.

title: Agents Under Siege: Breaking Pragmatic Multi-Agent LLM Systems with Optimized Prompt Attacks
org: University of North Carolina at Chapel Hill; Arizona State University; Cisco
abstract: This work attacks pragmatic multi-agent LLM systems that have real constraints: limited token bandwidth, message latency, and distributed safety mechanisms. It designs a permutation-invariant adversarial attack that optimizes prompt distribution across latency- and bandwidth-constrained network topologies to bypass distributed safety. The attack path is formulated as a maximum-flow minimum-cost problem, coupled with a novel Permutation-Invariant Evasion Loss (PIEL), leveraging graph-based optimization to maximize attack success while minimizing detection risk. Across Llama, Mistral, Gemma, DeepSeek-R1 variants on JailbreakBench, AdversarialBench, and In-the-wild Jailbreak Prompts, it outperforms conventional attacks by up to 7x; existing defenses (Llama-Guard variants, PromptGuard) fail to prohibit it.

title: Riddle Me This! Stealthy Membership Inference for Retrieval-Augmented Generation
org: University of Massachusetts Amherst; Northeastern University
abstract: Introduces Interrogation Attack (IA), a black-box membership inference attack against RAG datastores that crafts natural-text queries answerable only with the target document, achieving near-perfect inference with ~30 queries while evading off-the-shelf prompt-injection/jailbreak detectors. Reports 2x TPR@1%FPR improvement over prior RAG inference attacks at <$0.02/document, with detection rates as low as 5% vs ~90% for prior attacks.

title: AgentSentinel: An End-to-End and Real-Time Security Defense Framework for Computer-Use Agents
abstract: Proposes AgentSentinel, an end-to-end real-time security defense for computer-use agents that intercepts sensitive OS operations (process/file/network) via eBPF+LSM tracing and a hybrid rule-based + LLM-based auditor that correlates task context with system traces. Presents BadComputerUse, a benchmark of 60 attack scenarios across seven attack categories (avg ASR 87% on 4 SOTA LLMs). AgentSentinel achieves avg defense success rate 79.6% (up to 96.7% with Claude 3.7 Sonnet), FPR 10.8%, defends 17/20 adaptive attacks.

title: Automatic Red Teaming LLM-based Agents with Model Context Protocol Tools
venue: IEEE Transactions on Information Forensics and Security (TIFS) 2025
abstract: Proposes AutoMalTool, the first automated red-teaming framework that generates malicious MCP server packages (tool-poisoning attacks) from benign ones via a four-agent system (Initial Generator, Oracle, Effectiveness Evaluator, Tool Optimizer). Targets two malicious behaviors: incorrect parameter invocation (IPI) and output results manipulation (ORM). Evaluated on Claude Desktop and Cline across 53 MCP tools / 3 servers (Alpaca, WhatsApp, Filesystem): avg GSR ~85%, avg ESR 35.3% (>70% in some cases), cost ~$0.03/tool, <200s/tool. Evades MCP-Scan (detection 11.1%) and A.I.G (23.4%).

title: ThinkTrap: Denial-of-Service Attacks against Black-box LLM Services via Infinite Thinking
org: Shanghai Jiao Tong University; Donghua University
venue: Network and Distributed System Security Symposium (NDSS) 2026
abstract: Proposes ThinkTrap, a black-box input-space optimization DoS attack that crafts adversarial prompts inducing excessively long / non-terminating LLM reasoning to exhaust backend GPU compute. Maps discrete tokens to a continuous embedding space, applies derivative-free (CMA-ES) optimization in a low-dimensional subspace, and decodes via surrogate-vocabulary nearest-neighbor. Evaluated on 8 LLMs (GPT-o4, Gemini 2.5 Pro, DeepSeek R1, etc.); even at 10 RPM degrades throughput to as low as 1% of capacity, up to 100x latency, sometimes complete service failure, at ~$0.02 per attack.

title: Fun-tuning: Characterizing the Vulnerability of Proprietary LLMs to Optimization-based Prompt Injection Attacks via the Fine-Tuning Interface
org: UC San Diego; University of Wisconsin Madison
venue: IEEE Symposium on Security and Privacy (S&P) 2025
abstract: Surfaces a new graybox attack channel: the remote fine-tuning interface of closed-weight LLMs leaks a loss-like signal that an attacker can exploit (via a single very-small-learning-rate fine-tune iteration plus a de-randomization of the API's permuted losses) to guide discrete optimization of prompt-injection payloads. On the PurpleLlama (PPL40) benchmark, achieves 65% ASR on Gemini 1.5 Flash and 82% on Gemini 1.0 Pro, transferring across the Gemini family (>72-88% in some configs), at <$10 total / ~90 fine-tuning calls per example. Google deployed a mitigation in April 2025 (capped learning rate, min batch size 4).

title: Learning Safety Constraints for Large Language Models
abstract: Proposes SaP (Safety Polytope), a geometric, post-hoc approach that learns multiple safety constraints as the facets of a polytope in an LLM's representation space and enforces them via inference-time representation steering (SafeFlow), without modifying model weights. Frames LLM safety as a Constrained Markov Decision Process / convex-polytope learning problem. On HarmBench across 9 attacks and 3 LLMs (Llama2-7B, Ministral-8B, Qwen2-1.5B), reduces attack success rate (e.g., Llama2 12.92%->0.26%) while preserving MMLU accuracy; learned facets specialize to distinct semantic harm categories.

title: Know Thy Judge: On the Robustness Meta-Evaluation of LLM Safety Judges
venue: ICLR 2025 Workshop (I Can't Believe It's Not Better)
abstract: LLM-based judges underpin safety evaluation processes (offline benchmarking, automated red-teaming, online guardrailing). The paper highlights two overlooked challenges in safety-judge meta-evaluation: (i) evaluations in the wild (prompt sensitivity, distribution shift) and (ii) adversarial attacks targeting the judge. Small stylistic changes to model output cause jumps of up to 0.24 in false negative rate; adversarial output-level modifications can fool some judges into misclassifying 100% of harmful generations as safe, revealing that low attack success under a judge can create a false sense of security.

title: Exploring and Mitigating Adversarial Manipulation of Voting-Based Leaderboards
org: Google / UC Berkeley / CMU / Stanford / ETH Zurich
abstract: Voting-based LLM leaderboards (e.g., Chatbot Arena) rank models via crowdsourced anonymous pairwise votes and are widely trusted as fair capability measures. The paper shows that without bot protection and similar defenses, these benchmarks are vulnerable to adversarial manipulation. An attacker can alter the leaderboard (promote a favorite model or demote competitors) at the cost of roughly a thousand votes (verified in a simulated offline Chatbot Arena). The attack is two-step: (1) de-anonymize which model produced a reply with >95% accuracy, (2) consistently vote for/against a target. Working with the Chatbot Arena developers, they identify, propose and implement mitigations (Cloudflare bot protection, malicious-user detection, rate limiting, reCAPTCHA, login) that substantially raise attack cost.

title: SAeUron: Interpretable Concept Unlearning in Diffusion Models with Sparse Autoencoders
org: Warsaw University of Technology / IDEAS NCBR / IDEAS Research Institute
abstract: Diffusion models can inadvertently generate harmful or undesirable content. SAeUron is a machine-unlearning method that leverages features learned by sparse autoencoders (SAEs) to remove unwanted concepts in text-to-image diffusion models. SAEs trained unsupervised on activations from multiple denoising timesteps of Stable Diffusion capture sparse, interpretable concept-specific features; a score-based feature-selection method enables precise interventions on model activations to block targeted content while preserving overall performance. SAeUron outperforms prior methods on the UnlearnCanvas benchmark for concept and style unlearning, effectively eliminates nudity on I2P, supports removing multiple concepts with a single SAE, and—because SAEs are trained unsupervised—mitigates the possibility of generating unwanted content under adversarial attack.

title: Internal Activation Revision: Safeguarding Vision Language Models Without Parameter Update
org: Mohamed bin Zayed University of Artificial Intelligence / Fraunhofer FOKUS / University of Tokyo / University of Alberta
abstract: Vision-language models (VLMs) are more susceptible than their backbone LLMs to generating harmful content. The integration of images significantly shifts internal activations during the forward pass, diverging from text-only inputs, and the inherited LLM safety alignment is not robust to these activation discrepancies, leaving VLMs vulnerable to even the simplest jailbreaking attacks. The paper proposes internal activation revision, a training-free approach that revises activations during generation (at layer and head granularity) to steer the model toward safer outputs, using positive/negative sample revision vectors. The method reduces attack success rates by 48.94%, 34.34%, 43.92%, and 52.98% on SafeBench, Safe-Unsafe, Unsafe, and MM-SafetyBench respectively, while minimally impacting helpfulness.

title: CLIPure: Purification in Latent Space via CLIP for Adversarially Robust Zero-Shot Classification
org: State Key Lab of AI Safety, Institute of Computing Technology, Chinese Academy of Sciences / University of Chinese Academy of Sciences
abstract: The paper builds an adversarially robust zero-shot image classifier grounded on CLIP, using adversarial purification (no adversarial training, so it can cope with unforeseen attacks). It formulates purification risk as the KL divergence between the purification (denoising) and attack (perturbing) processes via bidirectional Stochastic Differential Equations, motivating purification in CLIP's multi-modal latent space. Two variants: CLIPure-Diff (models image latent likelihood with DaLLE-2's DiffusionPrior) and CLIPure-Cos (models likelihood via cosine similarity between image embedding and 'a photo of a.' text embedding — the first purification method not based on generative models). CLIPure boosts SOTA robustness from 71.7% to 91.1% on CIFAR-10, 59.6% to 72.6% on ImageNet, and gives 108% relative average-robustness improvement across 13 datasets.

title: Disentangling Adversarial Prompts: A Semantic-Graph Defense for Robust LLM Security
org: Huazhong University of Science and Technology / Nanyang Technological University
abstract: LLMs are vulnerable to adversarial prompts that exploit semantic ambiguities to bypass safety mechanisms (jailbreaking, prompt injection). The paper proposes the Adversarial Prompt Disentanglement (APD) framework, a proactive defense that identifies and neutralizes malicious components in input prompts before they reach the LLM. APD integrates three innovations: (1) a mutual-information-based semantic decomposition (VAE) that isolates adversarial and benign prompt components by minimizing their mutual information for statistical independence; (2) a graph-based intent classification using spectral analysis (semantic graph Laplacian, Cheeger's inequality) to detect malicious patterns; and (3) a lightweight transformer-based Adversarial Intent Detector trained on real-world toxic/jailbreaking datasets. APD reduces harmful output generation by over 85% while maintaining negligible impact on model performance, supporting real-time deployment.

title: Exploring User Security and Privacy Attitudes and Concerns Toward the Use of General-Purpose LLM Chatbots for Mental Health
abstract: Qualitative study (21 semi-structured interviews, U.S. adults, Aug-Sep 2024) of users' security & privacy attitudes toward general-purpose LLM chatbots (ChatGPT, Pi, Replika, Gemini, Copilot, My AI) used for mental health support. Identifies critical misconceptions: users conflate LLM human-like empathy with accountability, mistakenly believe interactions are HIPAA-protected, and undervalue 'intangible vulnerability' (emotional/psychological disclosures vs financial/location data). Proposes harm-reduction framework: contextual just-in-time warnings, strong default protections/ephemeral storage, targeted oversight/audits.

title: Unmasking Deceptive Visuals: Benchmarking Multimodal Large Language Models on Misleading Chart Question Answering
org: The Hong Kong University of Science and Technology
abstract: Introduces Misleading ChartQA benchmark: 3,026 curated multimodal MCQ examples spanning 21 misleader types and 10 chart types, each with standardized D3.js chart code, CSV data, MCQ, and labeled explanations. Built via a misleader taxonomy (4 groups: manipulated data, annotation, visual encoding, scale), seed MCQ design, GPT-4o-driven augmentation, and intensive expert validation (20 PhD students, $30/hr, 3-stage). Benchmarks 24 SOTA MLLMs; proposes a Region-Aware Misleader Reasoning (RAMR) pipeline. Finds models score ~40% (vs ~90% on standard ChartQA), are more misled by misleading distractors than generic ones, and weakest on scale manipulations.

title: How to Protect Yourself from 5G Radiation? Investigating LLM Responses to Implicit Misinformation
abstract: Introduces ECHOMIST, the first comprehensive benchmark for implicit misinformation: false assumptions embedded as unchallenged premises in user queries to LLMs. Curated from real human-LLM conversations (WildChat, LMSYS-Chat-1M), social media (Snopes-traced), and LLM-rewritten queries; 2,691 queries (2,085 implicit) over 216 misinformation claims, 5 query-type taxonomy. Evaluates 15 SOTA LLMs via a Claude-3.5-Sonnet LLM-as-judge (r=0.92 with humans). Finds models perform alarmingly poorly: reinforce implicit misinformation in 25.8%-57% of cases, worse on post-training-cutoff claims. Proposes Self-Alert and RAG mitigations (GPT-4 +13.4% / +15.7%).

title: SweEval: Do LLMs Really Swear? A Safety Benchmark for Testing Limits for Enterprise Use
org: Oracle AI / IIIT Ranchi / TD Securities / Columbia University / Hanyang University
abstract: Introduces SweEval, the first cross-lingual enterprise-safety benchmark testing whether LLMs comply with or resist explicit instructions to include swear words while completing enterprise communication tasks (emails, sales pitches, research drafts) across tone (positive/negative) and context (formal/informal). 109 English prompts x 25 swear words across 8 languages (English, Spanish, French, German, Hindi, Marathi, Bengali, Gujarati) = 2,725 prompts/language; two cases (multilingual + transliterated swearing). Evaluates 13 open-source LLMs (Mistral, Phi, Qwen, Llama; 7B-141B). Metric: Harmful Rate. Finds high harmful rates, worse in Indic/low-resource languages (Latin avg 0.46-0.63 vs Indic 0.62-0.79) and with transliterated swears.

title: The Jailbreak Tax: How Useful are Your Jailbreak Outputs?
abstract: Proposes the 'jailbreak tax' — the degradation in model utility that occurs when circumventing safety guardrails — as a new metric for AI safety. Builds jailbreak evaluation sets on objectively verifiable tasks (WMDP bio-security MCQ, GSM8K and MATH math reasoning) by aligning/pseudo-aligning models to refuse benign topics (via system prompt, SFT, or the new EvilMath dataset), then jailbreaking. Evaluates 8 representative jailbreaks (system-prompt JB, finetuning, GCG, AutoDAN, many-shot, MultiJail, PAIR, TAP) across LLaMA 3.1 8B/70B/405B and Claude 3.5 Haiku. Finds jailbreak success rate does not correlate with jailbreak tax; some attacks (PAIR) cut accuracy up to 92%.

title: ELBA-Bench: An Efficient Learning Backdoor Attacks Benchmark for Large Language Models
org: Wuhan University / National University of Singapore / Beihang University / Nanyang Technological University
abstract: Establishes ELBA-Bench, a comprehensive unified backdoor-attack benchmark for LLMs under two efficient-learning paradigms: parameter-efficient fine-tuning (PEFT, e.g. LoRA) and without-fine-tuning (W/o FT, e.g. in-context learning). Covers 12 attack methods, 18 datasets, 12 LLMs (open+closed), 1300+ experiments, 5 evaluation metrics (CACC, ASR, FTR, RR, PassR) and 2 stealthiness measures (semantic change, perplexity change). Key findings: PEFT attacks outperform W/o-FT in classification with strong cross-dataset generalization; BadChain achieves universal dominance in knowledge-reasoning; stronger reasoning LLMs are paradoxically MORE vulnerable to chain-of-thought backdoors; PoisonRAG dominates QA (>90% ASR in 27 combos).

title: Jailbreaking Multimodal Large Language Models via Shuffle Inconsistency
org: Institute of Artificial Intelligence, Beihang University; Alibaba Group
abstract: MLLMs exhibit a 'Shuffle Inconsistency' between comprehension ability and safety ability for shuffled harmful instructions: MLLMs can still understand shuffled harmful text-image instructions, but their defense mechanisms can be easily bypassed by the shuffled inputs, leading to harmful responses. The authors propose SI-Attack, a query-based black-box optimization jailbreak using a toxic judge model to select the most harmful shuffled inputs, improving attack success rate on commercial closed-source MLLMs such as GPT-4o and Claude-3.5-Sonnet.

title: Playing the Fool: Jailbreaking LLMs and Multimodal LLMs with Out-of-Distribution Strategy
org: NAVER Cloud ImageVision; KAIST; Republic of Korea Naval Academy; AITRICS
abstract: The paper investigates the vulnerability of safety alignment to out-of-distribution (OOD) harmful inputs that fall outside the aligned data distribution. Key observation: OOD-ifying vanilla harmful inputs highly increases the model's uncertainty in discerning malicious intent, raising the chance of being jailbroken. The authors propose JOOD, a black-box jailbreak framework that OOD-ifies harmful inputs via off-the-shelf visual and textual transformations (text-mixing, image mixup/CutMix). JOOD jailbreaks proprietary LLMs and MLLMs including GPT-4 and o1 with high ASR, achieving 63% ASR against GPT-4V in Bombs/Explosives and +42% ASR vs SOTA baseline in Hacking.

title: Visual Contextual Attack: Jailbreaking MLLMs with Image-Driven Context Injection
org: Shanghai Artificial Intelligence Laboratory; Purdue University
abstract: Defines a novel 'vision-centric jailbreak' setting where visual information serves as a necessary component in constructing a complete and realistic jailbreak scenario, not merely a trigger. Proposes the VisCo (Visual Contextual) Attack, which fabricates a deceptive multi-turn dialogue context using four vision-focused strategies, dynamically generating auxiliary images, then applies automatic toxicity obfuscation and semantic refinement. VisCo achieves toxicity 4.78 and ASR 85% on MM-SafetyBench against GPT-4o (vs QR baseline 2.48/22.2%), and 4.88/91.07% on Gemini-2.0-Flash.

title: Align is not Enough: Multimodal Universal Jailbreak Attack against Multimodal Large Language Models
org: Hefei University of Technology; Tsinghua University; Institute of Automation CAS; Nanyang Technological University
venue: IEEE Transactions on Circuits and Systems for Video Technology (TCSVT) 2025
abstract: Proposes a unified multimodal universal jailbreak attack framework that leverages iterative image-text interactions and a transfer-based strategy to generate a universal adversarial suffix and image. The work shows that multimodal universal jailbreak attacks bring higher-quality undesirable generations across different MLLMs, validating that multimodal interaction is a critical vulnerability and that current safety alignment is inadequate against sophisticated multimodal attacks. Evaluated on LLaVA, Yi-VL, MiniGPT4, MiniGPT-v2, InstructBLIP and transferred across 17 MLLMs.

title: Unveiling the Fragility of Vision-Language Models: Multi-Modal Adversarial Synergy via Texture-Constrained Perturbations and Cross-Modal Optimization
org: Huazhong University of Science and Technology; Nanyang Technological University; University College London
abstract: Introduces Multi-Modal Adversarial Synergy (MMAS), the first black-box, universal, multi-modal adversarial attack framework against Large Vision-Language Models (LVLMs). MMAS simultaneously generates a texture scale-constrained Universal Adversarial Perturbation (UAP) for images (wavelet-based, l_inf-bounded, visually imperceptible) and a learnable prompt perturbation for text (l_2-norm in embedding space), optimized jointly using only model queries. A novel cross-modal regularization term aligns the perturbations' gradient directions, enhancing synergistic impact and transferability across tasks and models. MMAS can force an LVLM to misclassify a 'stop sign' image paired with a 'proceed' prompt as 'go', threatening autonomous driving and content moderation.

title: X-Transfer Attacks: Towards Super Transferable Adversarial Attacks on CLIP
org: University of Melbourne; Singapore Management University; Fudan University
abstract: Introduces X-Transfer, a novel attack that generates a Universal Adversarial Perturbation (UAP) capable of deceiving various CLIP encoders and downstream VLMs across different samples, tasks, and domains simultaneously — a property the authors term 'super transferability' (cross-data, cross-domain, cross-model, and cross-task). This is achieved via efficient surrogate scaling that dynamically selects a small subset of suitable surrogate CLIP encoders from a large search space using a multi-armed-bandit / UCB strategy. X-Transfer significantly outperforms prior UAP methods and establishes the X-TransferBench benchmark.

title: InjecAgent: Benchmarking Indirect Prompt Injections in Tool-Integrated Large Language Model Agents
abstract: InjecAgent is the first benchmark to assess the vulnerability of tool-integrated LLM agents to indirect prompt injection (IPI) attacks. It comprises 1,054 test cases covering 17 user tools and 62 attacker tools, categorizing attack intentions into direct harm and data exfiltration. Evaluating 30 LLM agents, ReAct-prompted GPT-4 is vulnerable 24% of the time, rising to 47% in an enhanced setting where attacker instructions are reinforced with a hacking prompt.

title: Attacking Vision-Language Computer Agents via Pop-ups
org: Georgia Tech / University of Hong Kong / Stanford University
abstract: This work demonstrates that VLM-based computer agents can be easily attacked by carefully designed adversarial pop-ups that human users would typically recognize and ignore. The distraction leads agents to click the pop-ups instead of performing their tasks. Integrating these pop-ups into OSWorld and VisualWebArena yields an average attack success rate of 86% (OSWorld) / 73.1% (VisualWebArena) and decreases task success rate by 47%. Basic defenses (ignore-pop-up prompts, advertisement notices) are ineffective.

title: The Task Shield: Enforcing Task Alignment to Defend Against Indirect Prompt Injection in LLM Agents
org: Pennsylvania State University / Princeton University / California State University, Long Beach
abstract: Task Shield reframes agent security from preventing harmful actions to ensuring task alignment — every agent action must serve user objectives, asking 'Does this serve the intended task?' rather than 'Is this harmful?'. It is a test-time defense that systematically verifies whether each instruction and tool call contributes to user-specified goals. On the AgentDojo benchmark, Task Shield reduces attack success rates to 2.07% while maintaining 69.79% task utility on GPT-4o, outperforming existing defenses.

title: ATM: Adversarial Tuning Multi-agent System Makes a Robust Retrieval-Augmented Generator
abstract: ATM is an Adversarial Tuning Multi-agent system that hardens a retrieval-augmented Generator against noisy and LLM-fabricated documents in RAG-QA. An auxiliary Attacker agent fabricates misleading documents (Fabrication Generation) and shuffles document order (List Permutation) to maximize the Generator's perplexity; the Generator is iteratively tuned via a Multi-agent Iterative Tuning Optimization (MITO) loss to discriminate useful documents amid fabrications. After several adversarial rounds the Generator outperforms RAG robustness baselines (RetRobust, RAAT, REAR, Self-RAG).

title: Breaking ReAct Agents: Foot-in-the-Door Attack Will Get You In
abstract: This work introduces the Foot-in-the-Door (FITD) attack on ReAct LLM agents: an indirect prompt injection is prefaced by a small, harmless, unrelated request (a distractor, e.g. a basic calculation) that establishes a 'foot in the door', getting both the benign and malicious actions into the agent's thought process. Because a ReAct agent seldom re-evaluates an action once it enters its thought, the distractor significantly increases the likelihood of executing the subsequent malicious action — raising attack success rate by up to 44.8%. A reflection-based defense is proposed to mitigate it.

title: Reasoning Robustness of LLMs to Adversarial Typographical Errors
org: National University of Singapore / Singapore University of Technology and Design / Google DeepMind
abstract: This work studies the robustness of Chain-of-Thought (CoT) reasoning in LLMs to typographical errors that naturally occur in users' queries. It introduces the Adversarial Typo Attack (ATA), a gradient-guided algorithm that iteratively samples realistic typos for query words important to the model and selects the edit most likely to make the model fail. With 1 character edit, Mistral-7B-Instruct accuracy drops from 43.7% to 38.6% on GSM8K, and 8 edits halve it to 19.2%. The R2ATA benchmark applies ATA to GSM8K, BBH, and MMLU and shows transferable performance drops across large and closed-source LLMs.

title: Is LLM-as-a-Judge Robust? Investigating Universal Adversarial Attacks on Zero-shot LLM Assessment
abstract: First study on adversarial robustness of LLM-as-a-judge zero-shot assessment. Short universal adversarial phrases concatenated to candidate responses inflate scores. A surrogate attack (learn on FlanT5-3B, transfer to unseen judge-LLMs) drastically inflates scores irrespective of input text. Judge-LLMs are far more susceptible for absolute scoring than comparative assessment. Perplexity is explored as an initial detection defence.

title: BEEAR: Embedding-based Adversarial Removal of Safety Backdoors in Instruction-tuned Language Models
org: Virginia Tech / Georgia Tech / UC Berkeley / University of Chicago
abstract: BEEAR mitigates safety-backdoor attacks in instruction-tuned LLMs via the insight that backdoor triggers induce a relatively uniform drift in the model's embedding space. A bi-level optimization (Backdoor Embedding Entrapment + Adversarial Removal) identifies universal embedding perturbations eliciting unwanted behaviors and fine-tunes parameters to reinforce safe behaviors against them. Reduces RLHF-time backdoor ASR from >95% to <1% and instruction-tuning-time code backdoors from 47% to 0% without compromising utility, requiring only defender-defined safe/unsafe behaviors and no trigger-format assumptions.

title: Steering Away from Harm: An Adaptive Approach to Defending Vision Language Model Against Jailbreaks
abstract: ASTRA is an efficient, effective defense that adaptively steers Vision Language Models away from adversarial feature directions to resist jailbreaks. Transferable steering vectors representing the direction of harmful response are built by randomly ablating visual tokens of adversarial images and identifying those most associated with jailbreaks; adaptive activation steering via projection between steering vectors and calibrated activations is applied at inference. ASTRA achieves SOTA with little benign-performance drop and good transferability to unseen attacks (structured-based, PGD variants, text-only).

title: Defending Jailbreak Prompts via In-Context Adversarial Game
org: University of Notre Dame / INRIA / KAUST
abstract: ICAG defends against jailbreaks without fine-tuning by running an in-context adversarial game between an attack agent and a defense agent that iteratively co-evolve via agent learning (reflection + insight extraction). The defense agent produces a single safety-enhancing system prompt. ICAG reduces Jailbreak Success Rate by an average 7.99% over the best baseline across ten unseen attacks on four defense LLMs and transfers across LLMs with only a 2.86% average JSR increase.

title: TAPT: Test-Time Adversarial Prompt Tuning for Robust Inference in Vision-Language Models
abstract: TAPT is the first inference-time (test-time) adversarial defense for pre-trained VLMs such as CLIP. It learns defensive bimodal (textual+visual) prompts per test sample, unsupervised, by minimizing a multi-view entropy and aligning adversarial-clean embedding distributions against pre-computed public-dataset (ImageNet) statistics. Across 11 datasets it enhances CLIP's zero-shot adversarial robustness by >=48.9% against AutoAttack while largely maintaining clean performance, and outperforms existing adversarial prompt-tuning methods by an average of at least 36.6%.

title: Images are Achilles' Heel of Alignment: Exploiting Visual Vulnerabilities for Jailbreaking Multimodal Large Language Models
abstract: Empirical analysis of MLLM harmlessness alignment showing the image input poses an alignment vulnerability, plus HADES — a jailbreak that hides and amplifies harmful intent within meticulously crafted images. Achieves average ASR of 90.26% on LLaVA-1.5 and 71.60% on Gemini Pro Vision.

title: ImgTrojan: Jailbreaking Vision-Language Models with ONE Image
abstract: A data-poisoning jailbreak against VLMs: poisoned (image, text) pairs replace original captions with malicious jailbreak prompts in the training set. Poisoning one image among 10,000 raises ASR by 51.2% absolute; with <100 poisoned samples ASR reaches 83.5%, while clean-image captioning degrades minimally. Studies poison ratio, trainable-parameter locus, persistence, and stealth.

title: Jailbreak Large Vision-Language Models Through Multi-Modal Linkage
org: Institute of Information Engineering, Chinese Academy of Sciences / Tsinghua University / University of Chicago
abstract: Multi-Modal Linkage (MML) is a structure-based jailbreak for SOTA closed-source VLMs. Inspired by cryptography, it applies an encryption-decryption process across text and image modalities to mitigate over-exposure of malicious content, plus 'evil alignment' that frames the attack as a video-game development scenario. MML jailbreaks GPT-4o at 99.40% on SafeBench, 98.81% on MM-SafeBench, and 99.07% on HADES-Dataset.

title: Audio Is the Achilles' Heel: Red Teaming Audio Large Multimodal Models
abstract: First systematic red teaming of five audio LMMs (Qwen-Audio, Qwen2-Audio, SALMONN-7B/13B, Gemini-1.5-Pro) under three settings: harmful questions in audio+text, harmful text with distracting non-speech audio, and speech-specific jailbreaks. Open-source audio LMMs show an average 69.14% ASR on harmful audio questions and safety drops when distracted by non-speech noise; a speech-specific jailbreak achieves 70.67% ASR on Gemini-1.5-Pro.

title: One Prompt Word is Enough to Boost Adversarial Robustness of Vision-Language Models
org: King's College London / Imperial College London
abstract: Studies adversarial robustness of pre-trained CLIP-like VLMs from the text-prompt perspective (weights frozen). Shows both adversarial attack and defense are sensitive to the text prompt, then proposes Adversarial Prompt Tuning (APT) — learning a robust text prompt. Adding one learned word boosts accuracy +13% and robustness +8.5% over hand-engineered prompts (ε=4/255), up to +26.4%/+16.7% in the best setting, across 15 datasets and 4 data-sparsity schemes.

title: Know Your Limits: A Survey of Abstention in Large Language Models
org: University of Washington / Allen Institute for AI
abstract: Survey framing abstention (refusal to answer) as a safety/reliability meta-capability, analyzed from three perspectives — query answerability a(x), model confidence/knowledge c(x,y), and human-value alignment h(x),h(x,y). Organizes abstention methods by LLM lifecycle stage (pretraining/alignment/inference) and surveys benchmarks and metrics, identifying gaps including over-abstention, abstention manipulation, and demographic bias.

title: How Johnny Can Persuade LLMs to Jailbreak Them: Rethinking Persuasion to Challenge AI Safety by Humanizing LLMs
org: Virginia Tech / Renmin University of China / UC Davis / Stanford
abstract: Introduces a persuasion taxonomy (40 techniques, 13 strategies) from decades of social science to automatically paraphrase plain harmful queries into human-readable Persuasive Adversarial Prompts (PAP). PAP achieves >92% attack success rate on Llama-2-7b-Chat, GPT-3.5, and GPT-4 within 10 trials without specialized optimization, surpassing recent algorithm-focused attacks. A significant gap exists in current post-hoc defenses against PAP; the authors propose adaptive defenses (adaptive system prompt, base/tuned summarizer).

title: ArtPrompt: ASCII Art-based Jailbreak Attacks against Aligned LLMs
org: University of Washington / UIUC / Western Washington University / University of Chicago
abstract: Current LLM safety alignment presumes corpora are interpreted solely by semantics. ArtPrompt exploits LLMs' poor ability to recognize ASCII art (quantified by a new Vision-in-Text Challenge, ViTC, benchmark) to mask safety-trigger words and bypass alignment. A two-step black-box attack (word masking + cloaked ASCII-art prompt generation) induces unsafe behavior from GPT-3.5, GPT-4, Claude, Gemini, and Llama2, outperforming five SOTA jailbreaks on average and bypassing perplexity/paraphrase/retokenization defenses.

title: DrAttack: Prompt Decomposition and Reconstruction Makes Powerful LLM Jailbreakers
org: UCLA / Penn State / University of Maryland College Park
abstract: Existing jailbreaks treat the harmful prompt as a whole and fail to reduce LLM attention on combinations of malicious words. DrAttack introduces a fourth 'decomposition-based' category: it (a) decomposes a malicious prompt into benign sub-prompts via syntactic parsing, (b) implicitly reconstructs them via in-context learning with benign assembling examples, and (c) runs synonym search on sub-prompts. On GPT-4 it achieves >80% ASR (human eval), surpassing prior SOTA by 65% absolute, with merely ~15 queries, and bypasses real-world defenses (OpenAI Moderation, perplexity filter, RA-LLM, output filter).

title: Jailbreaking Prompt Attack: A Controllable Adversarial Attack against Diffusion Models
org: Zhejiang University / UC San Diego / ETH Zurich
abstract: Text-to-Image (T2I) diffusion models can be misused to generate NSFW content. JPA (Jailbreaking Prompt Attack) is a practical, universal, black-box attack that does not require a target model. It exploits the fact that the high-dimensional CLIP text embedding space inherently contains NSFW concepts: it searches a concept embedding via ChatGPT-generated antonyms, adds it to the prompt, then optimizes a discrete prefix prompt with a soft-assignment + gradient-masking technique. JPA bypasses both text and image safety checkers and concept-removal methods while preserving semantic alignment, and runs 4x faster than prior methods.

title: Distract Large Language Models for Automatic Jailbreak Attack
org: Shanghai University of Finance and Economics / Southern University of Science and Technology
abstract: DAP (Distraction-based Adversarial Prompts) is a black-box automatic jailbreak framework motivated by the distractibility and over-confidence phenomena of LLMs. It (1) conceals the malicious query as an auxiliary task inside a complex, unrelated main task to distract the model's safety attention, (2) uses a memory-reframing scheme that forces the target to begin its response with an affirmative string so it follows its own partial output, and (3) iteratively optimizes the jailbreak template with an attacker LLM and a fine-tuned DeBERTa judge. DAP achieves Top-1 ASR 66.7%/38.0% on ChatGPT/GPT-4 and transfers across models and queries.

title: Sowing the Wind, Reaping the Whirlwind: The Impact of Editing Language Models
org: Indian Institute of Technology Kharagpur / Singapore University of Technology and Design
abstract: Investigates how knowledge/model editing (ROME, MEMIT) affects LLM safety. Reveals a paradox: injecting sensitive-yet-accurate information to improve reliability can destabilize the model's guardrails, so a single correct edit can instigate unethical responses. Introduces NicheHazardQA (500 unethical questions across six sensitive topics) and shows editing is a cost-effective tool for topical red-teaming, with effects that are topic-centric/niche and persist within and across topical domains.
